calibration.domain: Great-power conflict, war, and geopolitical order

adjustments.justification: UNDER-forecast, and internally contradicted. The model's own continuous variable puts current Hormuz crude flow at 8 mb/d against a ~20 mb/d baseline - i.e. 40% of baseline, already BELOW the 50% threshold the discrete risk asks about. I verified corroborating reporting: CNBC (13 Jul 2026) treats ~8m bbl transiting under military escort as news, and Kpler shows transits pinned at ~3 vessels/day 22-24 July with Brent back near $100. So the analyst is pricing 58% on an event substantially occurring at the moment of forecast. The only thing between this and near-certainty is the 'episode beginning on or after 1 Aug 2026' clause - a scope trap he never addresses. Even on a strict re-start reading, with an unresolved war, an active US blockade since 14 July, mining/insurance withdrawal and the failed 60-day MoU deadline landing in August, 17 months without any 30-day sub-50% window is the unlikely branch. His contrarian case ('I am 25 points too high') points the wrong way.

Follows from the 2027 revision and fixes a hazard-shape defect: 58-70-76 implies ~25%/yr to 2027, then ~4%/yr in 2027-31 and ~1.5%/yr in 2031-36. That decay is far steeper than any plausible normalisation path for a Gulf with a decapitated Iranian leadership, no IAEA access and an established US blockade precedent. The coherent shape is a high near-term hazard decaying to a structurally elevated 4-5%/yr floor.
Same correction. A 2031-36 hazard of ~1.5%/yr sits below the analyst's own stated unconditional base rate (1-2%/yr) for a decade in which he explicitly assumes the Iran file remains unresolved.

SCOPE INSENSITIVITY. The bar is severe - 180 consecutive days, entire land front, no sustained offensives AND no systematic long-range strikes on cities. The reasoning argues the vibe ('the file is closing'), not the wording. His own evidence cuts against the criterion: Ukrainian officials publicly favour a PARTIAL ceasefire, which does not resolve YES, and the most likely 2026-27 outcome - a line freeze with continued deep-strike exchange - also does not resolve YES. A ceasefire must additionally START by roughly early July 2027 to bank 180 days. Historically, wars of this length rarely produce a clean 180-day stop at the first attempt. His contrarian ('I could easily be 15 points too high') is right and should have moved the number.

78% is inconsistent with the model's own continuous variables. geo_ukraine_monthly_territory_change gives p50_2031 = +8 km2/month and p90 = 175 - a median world with active Russian advance - and geo_battle_deaths_annual carries a drift of only -5k/yr while Ukraine is named the dominant fatality contributor. The notes gesture at regime-switching, but the stated quantiles are what a downstream model would use. 70% reconciles them at least cost.

BASE RATE VIOLATION against his own model. He specifies an ~8%/yr hazard in the 'postured but restrained' state; 17% by end-2027 over ~1.4 years implies ~13%/yr, 60% above his own parameter. Nine years of restraint through more provocative periods (2019 summit collapse, the 2022 record missile year, Russian alignment) is strong evidence for the low-hazard regime, and he notes Moscow does not want a test and then does not price it.

42% implies a sustained ~9%/yr against a nine-year observed drought - a posterior that essentially ignores the drought. Splitting his 8%/yr model and his own contrarian 3%/yr gives 4-5%/yr and ~25-30% by 2031. The deterrence-signalling substitution argument (ICBM flight tests deliver most of the signal at a fraction of the cost to the China relationship) is raised in his contrarian paragraph and then discarded.
Rescaled to a ~4%/yr long-run hazard. Preserves the correct declining-hazard shape while removing the level inflation.

COHERENCE. Iran-has-a-bomb is a strict subset of geopolitics_new_nuclear_weapons_state (6% by 2027). At 5 vs 6, only 1 point remains for ROK, Japan, Poland, Saudi Arabia and Taiwan combined - while the superset's own reasoning names ROK as the second-likeliest candidate, cites 75-80% ROK support, and the model runs a proliferation-cascade loop at strength 0.55. That is a near-conjunction violation. On the merits, 5% by end-2027 is also too high: the criterion needs a test, a declaration, or a public IAEA/USIC assessment of an ASSEMBLED weapon, from a state whose conversion and metallurgy infrastructure was destroyed twice and whose detected dash invites immediate re-strike - the ~2.5-year estimate he himself calls more credible.

Same nesting problem, less acute: 15 of 21 leaves 6 points for every other candidate over five years, thin given his own guarantor-withdrawal cascade. Cutting Iran to 12 leaves ~9 for the ROK/Poland/Saudi/Japan branch, matching the stated mechanism. Note also that the superset's base-rate arithmetic is wrong - he writes '~0.036/yr... I am pricing roughly 3-4x the recent base rate', but 0.036/yr over the 10 years to 2036 is ~30%, so 36% is ~1.2x. The superset levels are defensible; I leave them. It is the stated multiplier that is wrong, which means he does not know how much uplift he is applying.

Mild upward nudge for consistency with the revised 2031/2036 path. The November 2026 tariff-truce expiry is an identified forcing point inside this window, and the model's own text calls quarantine 'the option that maximises coercive effect while minimising the chance of triggering a US shooting response'.

INTERNAL RATIO INCOHERENCE. Invasion 6% vs quarantine 14% by 2031 is a 0.43 ratio: it says the hardest amphibious operation in military history is nearly half as likely as the cheap, reversible, repeatedly-rehearsed option the model's own text says Beijing prefers. If quarantine really dominates on cost-benefit, 0.20-0.30 is the coherent range. The Jan-2028 Taiwan election and the Oct-2027 Party Congress both fall inside this window, and the 2026 Venezuela/Iran precedents lower Beijing's estimate of the cost of unilateral coercion via his own imitation loop. His contrarian says '25% is defensible'; 19% is the conservative version of acting on it.

HAZARD SHAPE. 14 to 22 over 2031-36 implies ~1.9%/yr, LOWER than the ~2.4%/yr implied for 2027-31, despite every structural driver (PLA capability accretion, Taiwanese identity trend, US burden-shifting) pointing the other way over the longer horizon. A flat-to-rising 2.5-3%/yr gives ~28%.

I checked Polymarket directly: 'China invade Taiwan by 31 Dec 2027' trades around 12% and 'by 30 Jun 2027' around 12.5%, against the model's 1.5% (the model's cited 14.5% is also slightly stale). Longshot bias plus the looser Polymarket resolution language - which many traders read as covering blockade or major military action rather than strictly an opposed landing of 1,000+ troops - explains most of an 8x gap, but not all of it. A 40-60% discount off 12% for criteria-tightening and longshot bias lands at 3-5%; 2.5% is a conservative move that still respects the ODNI 'no 2027 invasion plan' assessment while not sitting an order of magnitude under a well-capitalised market. The 2031 (6%) and 2036 (13%) figures are defensible and I leave them alone.

SCOPE INSENSITIVITY running opposite to the reasoning. The criterion requires 'an exchange of fire (kinetic, including missile, air, naval or ground fire)' producing a death. The reasoning then says the likely pathway is 'a fatal collision or water-cannon death' - neither is an exchange of fire and neither resolves YES. Strip the non-qualifying pathways and the number must fall. Base rate is zero force-on-force lethal exchanges in 47 years of continuous close contact, including the 2001 EP-3 fatality that he correctly notes would not have counted.

11% is ~2.3%/yr against an observed rate of zero in 47 years, justified by a mechanism that does not satisfy the wording. He also notes H1 2026 moved the wrong way for this risk in the good sense - Beijing summit, purchase commitments, both sides wanting the truce extended - and then leaves the number unchanged. 7% (~1.4%/yr) still prices a large uplift over base.

Proportional rescale, preserving the reasonable mildly-declining hazard shape while correcting the level for the exchange-of-fire wording. Note the resulting oddity in the original: US-PRC (11) and PRC-Japan (10) are priced almost identically at 2031 despite the Japan criterion explicitly including deliberate ramming - a materially broader trigger set. I leave the Japan numbers alone; they are defensible.

The reasoning makes the case for a lower number and then does not use it. NATO's revealed preference across 2014-2026 - Crimea, MH17, Salisbury, cable cuts, airport-closing drone incursions, Sandworm wipers on ~30 Polish energy sites - has been Article 4 every single time without exception, and Russian operations are engineered to stay under the threshold. Compounding this, invocation requires consensus, and a US administration mid-drawdown is the least likely in NATO's history to grant it. 9% implies ~1.9%/yr against a 77-year record of one invocation, and that one not against a state.
Proportional rescale, and consistent with his own claim that a Ukraine settlement (70-78% by 2031) reduces the Russia-NATO pretext - which should bend the 2031-36 hazard down more than 9-to-14 does.

Severity 10 encodes 'Article 5 means general war', which his own reasoning explicitly rejects: 'a formal invocation does not require war - it could be invoked for a limited response, which makes it cheaper and thus more likely.' He cannot have it both ways. If the probability is raised because invocation can be cheap and narrow, the severity conditional on invocation must fall to a mixture of narrow-response and general-war branches.

UNDER-forecast via scope insensitivity in the permissive direction - the clearest case in the model of a slow institutional move being under-rated. The criterion counts a 'formal reciprocal political commitment announced by both heads of state' setting a numerical ceiling: no ratification, no verification, no Senate. Putin has already publicly floated one-year reciprocal adherence to New START central limits, and Trump has repeatedly advertised personal interest in a denuclearisation headline. That is exactly the low-cost, summit-friendly instrument this wording catches, and it requires solving neither Golden Dome nor Chinese trilateralisation - those block a real treaty, not a communique. His own contrarian says 'my 2027 number could be double.'

Over five and a half years spanning a probable Ukraine settlement (his own near-necessary precondition, priced at 70-78%), a US presidential election, and mutual fiscal pressure against an uncapped race, 30% is low for an instrument this cheap to sign. Conditional on detente onset, the historical pattern is that strategic arms talks conclude within 2-4 years (1969-72, 1985-87, 1989-91 all fit).

Six agreements in 54 years is about one per nine years unconditional. A full decade with zero cap of any kind, including a mere political commitment, would be the longest such gap since 1972 and should not be the modal outcome at 57%.

BASE RATE VIOLATION - the worst offender in the model. The threshold is one million people for 24 consecutive hours. The entire historical record of cyber-caused blackouts is Ukraine 2015 (~230k customers, ~6 hours) and Kyiv 2016 (~1 hour): two to three orders of magnitude short on the population-times-duration product, achieved against the most exposed large grid in Europe after years of pre-positioned access. Nothing in the cited 2025-26 evidence (Sandworm wipers on IT systems at Polish energy firms, CISA PLC advisories, Volt Typhoon pre-positioning) has produced a single sustained outage anywhere. He identifies the binding constraint - restoration is manual and Western operators drill it - and then prices 6% in 17 months anyway.

20% is ~4%/yr against an unconditional rate he himself puts at 'well under 1%/yr', with no intermediate-scale precedent to interpolate from. The missing intermediate observation is decisive: at a true 4%/yr hazard for the 1M/24h event we should already have seen multiple 100k-people/6h events in NATO states, and we have seen zero. 11% still embeds a large uplift for a Russia-NATO or Iran-endgame decision to cross the threshold.

33% is a one-in-three claim about an event class with zero instances anywhere on earth at that scale in the ~11 years since the capability was first demonstrated. Omitted offsets: grid operators are hardening at roughly the rate attackers improve, NIS2 and NERC CIP requirements bind, and adversaries destroy irreplaceable access by using it - a point he raises and then does not price.

The criterion is strict - abolition of the office, vacancy over 90 days, or a non-clerical/non-IRGC government controlling Tehran. The single likeliest 'change' scenario, an IRGC-dominated hollowing-out with Mojtaba as figurehead, resolves NO. His own base-rate note says almost no comparable regime fell within 18 months absent an occupying ground force, and there is none; his own consolidation feedback loop is balancing on a 1-2 year horizon; and he writes that instability should peak in 2027-2029. All three arguments point below 11% for the near date.

Modest trim for criterion strictness and the absence of an organised successor coalition, which he correctly identifies as the usual binding constraint. The direction and shape of this forecast are among the better ones in the model and I leave most of it intact.
Proportional trim. The 2031-36 implied hazard (~2%/yr) is already reasonable and is one of the few well-shaped curves here.

This requires a Charter amendment ratified by two-thirds of members INCLUDING all five permanent members - China ratifying India's or Japan's permanent seat, and Russia ratifying a Western-aligned addition, during the most acute great-power confrontation since 1983. In 81 years, Council composition has been amended once (1965, non-permanent seats only) and permanent membership has never changed except by state succession. 2.5% over 5.5 years is ~0.45%/yr, roughly 4x the historical rate for a strictly easier amendment, at the moment of minimum comity.

6% implies ~0.7%/yr and would make this decade roughly as likely to deliver expansion as the entire post-war period combined. His own reasoning says the 2026 environment 'increases the rhetorical demand for reform while decreasing the great-power comity needed to deliver it' - an argument for going below the historical base rate, not four times above it. The one legitimate upward consideration he raises (a resolver counting veto-less permanent seats as YES) is a wording ambiguity to fix in the criterion, not something to pay for with probability.

coherence_violations: NESTING / NEAR-CONJUNCTION VIOLATION: geopolitics_iran_nuclear_weapon (5 / 15 / 23) is a strict subset of geopolitics_new_nuclear_weapons_state (6 / 21 / 36). At 2027 that leaves 1 percentage point for ROK, Japan, Poland, Saudi Arabia and Taiwan combined - while the superset's own reasoning names ROK as the second-most-likely candidate, cites 75-80% ROK public support and a Polish presidential endorsement, and the model carries a 'guarantor-withdrawal to proliferation cascade' loop at strength 0.55. As written the model asserts that essentially all near-term proliferation risk is Iranian, contradicting its own narrative.

DISCRETE/CONTINUOUS CONTRADICTION ON HORMUZ: geo_hormuz_crude_flow sets current_value = 8 mb/d against a stated ~20 mb/d baseline - 40% of baseline, i.e. already below the 50% threshold that geopolitics_hormuz_major_closure asks about - yet that risk is priced at 58% for a qualifying 30-day episode over the following 17 months. The model simultaneously asserts the event is happening now and that its recurrence is a coin flip. Externally corroborated: CNBC 13 Jul 2026 treats ~8m bbl/day transiting under military escort as news, and Kpler shows transits at ~3 vessels/day on 22-24 July with Brent back near $100 - which also contradicts the state_of_play's claim that markets are pricing normalisation.

UNADDRESSED SCOPE TRAP IN THE SAME RISK: the criterion requires 'an episode beginning on or after 1 August 2026'. If the current disruption runs continuously across 1 August, a strict resolver scores it NO no matter how bad flows get; a loose resolver scores it YES immediately. That is a swing of more than 50 points hiding in one clause, and the reasoning never mentions it.

CEASEFIRE PROBABILITY vs CONTINUOUS VARIABLES: geopolitics_ukraine_durable_ceasefire at 78% by 2031 is inconsistent with geo_ukraine_monthly_territory_change (p50_2031 = +8 km2/month, p90 = 175 km2/month - a median world with an advancing Russian army) and with geo_battle_deaths_annual carrying a drift of only -5k/yr while Ukraine is named the dominant fatality contributor. The notes fields wave at 'regime-switching' but the stated quantiles are what any downstream model consumes.

STATED BASE-RATE ARITHMETIC CONTRADICTS THE STATED NUMBER: geopolitics_new_nuclear_weapons_state says 'only one in the last 28 years (~0.036/yr). I am pricing roughly 3-4x the recent base rate.' 0.036/yr compounded over the 10 years to 2036 is ~30%; the model's 36% is ~1.2x, not 3-4x. The forecast is defensible but the justification is numerically wrong, meaning the analyst does not know how much uplift he is actually applying - and the same loose arithmetic recurs in the DPRK and Article 5 anchors.

RESOLUTION-CRITERION vs MECHANISM MISMATCH (geopolitics_us_china_lethal_clash): the criterion requires 'an exchange of fire' producing a death; the reasoning's primary pathways are 'a fatal collision or water-cannon death' and Chinese coast guard ramming, none of which is an exchange of fire. The probability is being set by scenarios that cannot resolve the question YES. The mirror defect: geopolitics_china_japan_lethal_clash DOES include deliberate ramming in its criterion, yet the two are priced almost identically (11 vs 10 at 2031) despite one having a materially broader trigger set.

IMPLAUSIBLE INTERNAL RATIO ON TAIWAN: invasion 6% vs quarantine 14% by 2031 = 0.43. The model argues at length that quarantine is cheap, reversible, rehearsed and dominant, and that an opposed landing is 'the hardest military operation in the world'. A dominance argument that strong is incompatible with a 0.43 ratio; 0.20-0.30 is coherent. Compounding it, no rung is modelled between the two (offshore-island seizure), so both numbers are absorbing probability mass belonging to an unmodelled middle option.

SYSTEMATIC HAZARD-SHAPE DEFECT: across at least six risks the implied 2031-36 annual hazard falls sharply below the 2027-31 hazard for no stated reason - Hormuz (25%/yr, then 4%/yr, then 1.5%/yr), DPRK test (13%, 8.7%, 5%), Taiwan quarantine (2.4% then 1.9%). Some decay is defensible where a named crisis resolves, but applying it near-uniformly is the signature of choosing cumulative numbers that 'look spaced' rather than integrating a hazard function - especially for events whose drivers (PLA capability, DPRK fissile output, uncapped post-New START arsenals) are structurally RISING. UNSC expansion is the lone case where the implied hazard rises (0.45%/yr to 0.7%/yr), and it is the one where the argument for decay is strongest.

MISSING PROBABILITY MASS ACROSS BRANCHES: for the Iran file the model prices regime change (26% by 2031) and weapon acquisition (15%) but has no risk for the far likelier intermediate outcomes - NPT withdrawal, a renewed strike campaign, or restored inspections. The branches sum to well under 100% with the residual undefined, so nothing disciplines the level of any single branch. The same absence of a shared driver means Hormuz closure, oil price, Russian sanctions revenue and Iranian regime survival are reported as independent marginals when they are one joint distribution.

missing_risks.name: A recognised nuclear-weapon state (US, Russia or China) conducts a nuclear explosive test
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: The United States, Russia or China conducts a supercritical nuclear explosive test (yield above zero, excluding subcritical and hydrodynamic experiments), confirmed by the testing state or by CTBTO/national technical means.
missing_risks.reasoning: The single largest omission, and astonishing given the model's own framing. The analyst builds his narrative around New START's expiry and the death of arms control, prices a seventh DPRK test at 42% by 2031, and then omits the live, verified, mainstream 2026 question. I confirmed by search: Trump publicly directed resumption of nuclear testing in Oct-Nov 2025; Putin ordered the Security Council to prepare proposals in response; the Novaya Zemlya site director has declared the site 'fully ready' and imagery shows construction and logistics activity; Russia has de-ratified the CTBT; and CSIS, the Cipher Brief and Russia Matters have all published on whether the moratorium survives the year. A US or Russian test is a larger discontinuity than a DPRK test - it ends a 34-year US and 36-year Russian moratorium, effectively kills the CTBT, and hands Beijing and Pyongyang immediate cover. I put ~20% by end-2027, 45% by 2031, ~55% by 2036, weighted toward the US moving first and Russia reciprocating within months.

missing_risks.name: Iran formally withdraws from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: Iran deposits formal notice of withdrawal under NPT Article X with the depositary governments and the UN Security Council, or that withdrawal takes effect.
missing_risks.reasoning: The model notes NPT-withdrawal legislation is live in the Majlis and that IAEA monitoring is near-totally lost, then prices only the terminal event (an assembled weapon, 15% by 2031). Withdrawal is a far cheaper and far likelier intermediate step: it is a political decision available tomorrow, requires no centrifuges, and is the natural response of a regime bombed while nominally compliant. It is also the highest-information single observable for the weapon track and the most plausible trigger for the cascade the model's own feedback loop describes. Without it the model has no rung between 'monitoring lost' and 'bomb confirmed'. ~25% by end-2027, 45% by 2031, ~50% by 2036.

missing_risks.name: A second US kinetic operation to remove or kill a sitting foreign head of state or government
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: US forces, after 1 August 2026, conduct a military operation that captures, kills, or directly precipitates within 30 days the removal from power of the sitting head of state or government of a UN member state, excluding the January 2026 Venezuela and February 2026 Iran operations.
missing_risks.reasoning: The model builds a 'successful-coercion imitation' loop (strength 0.45) explicitly around two US operations in six months that cost zero US casualties and drew condemnation only from states with no enforcement capacity - and then prices no discrete risk for the obvious implication that Washington does it again. Two instances in seven months is an observed rate that, even discounted hard for target availability and post-midterm congressional constraint, gives a substantial multi-year probability, and candidate targets are not hypothetical. This risk also carries most of the model's cross-risk correlation, which structural_uncertainties concedes is 'high and unmodelled' - an argument for modelling it, not for a prose caveat. ~15% by end-2027, 40% by 2031, ~50% by 2036.

missing_risks.name: PRC forces cause the death of a Philippine serviceman or coast guardsman
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: An action by PLA, PLAN, China Coast Guard or maritime-militia units (including ramming, water cannon, boarding or fire) directly causes at least one death among Philippine armed forces, coast guard or government-chartered personnel, confirmed by the Philippine government.
missing_risks.reasoning: The model treats the Philippines only as a sub-pathway inside geopolitics_us_china_lethal_clash and never prices the node that actually matters. A PRC-caused Filipino death is perhaps an order of magnitude likelier than a US-PRC exchange of fire - Second Thomas Shoal and Scarborough incidents have already produced a severed finger, blinded crews and rammed hulls, with rising tempo over four years - and it is the specific event that triggers the Mutual Defense Treaty consultations Washington has repeatedly said cover armed attacks on Philippine public vessels. Without it the model's Asia escalation ladder has no realistic bottom rung, which is why its US-PRC number ends up doing work its own wording forbids. ~15% by end-2027, 38% by 2031, ~50% by 2036.

missing_risks.name: PRC seizes or occupies a Taiwan-administered offshore island
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: PLA, PAP or China Coast Guard forces land on and establish administrative or military control over Pratas (Dongsha), Taiping (Itu Aba), Kinmen, Matsu or Wuqiu, maintained for at least 72 consecutive hours, confirmed by Taiwan MND or US government statement.
missing_risks.reasoning: The model's Taiwan ladder jumps from ADIZ sorties straight to a declared 7-day quarantine and then to a 1,000-man opposed landing, with nothing in between. Offshore-island seizure is the cheapest available fait accompli: Pratas sits 450 km from Taiwan proper, is garrisoned by a few hundred marines, is militarily indefensible, and is legally ambiguous enough that a US kinetic response is genuinely doubtful. Most war-gaming communities rate it the likeliest first PLA use of force. Its absence means the model cannot represent the scenario where Beijing tests the alliance at minimal risk - precisely the scenario its own imitation loop makes more likely after Caracas and Tehran. ~4% by end-2027, 13% by 2031, ~20% by 2036.

missing_risks.name: Vladimir Putin ceases to hold effective power in Russia
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: Putin ceases to serve as President of the Russian Federation, or is assessed by consensus of major-power governments no longer to exercise effective control over Russian state decision-making, for any reason including death, incapacity, resignation or removal.
missing_risks.reasoning: The model names this in structural_uncertainties as 'the largest single discontinuity risk for the Russia-Ukraine and Russia-NATO tracks' and lists the March 2030 election as a scheduled event, then declines to price it - exactly backwards for a risk that is both quantifiable and conditioning on nearly everything else in the domain. The actuarial baseline alone for a 73-year-old Russian male over 5.5 years is roughly 15-20%; adding non-trivial coup, incapacity and negotiated-exit hazard for a wartime personalist leader gives ~30-35% by 2031. It should be a conditioning variable on the Ukraine ceasefire, Article 5, arms-control and grid-cyber risks rather than a paragraph of prose. ~10% by end-2027, 32% by 2031, ~52% by 2036.

missing_risks.name: Renewed major US and/or Israeli air campaign against Iran
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: At least 100 US and/or Israeli strikes on targets inside Iran within any 30-day window beginning on or after 1 August 2026, per credible multi-source reporting or US/Israeli government statement.
missing_risks.reasoning: The whole state_of_play describes a war that has not ended: the 14 June MoU's 60-day deadline falls in August 2026, the US has paused rather than stopped strikes, Iran struck three commercial vessels in July, a naval blockade is in force, and with IAEA access gone any reconstitution is undetectable until it is large - which is itself a strike trigger. The model prices three downstream consequences (Hormuz closure, Iranian regime change, Iranian weapon) but never the proximate military event that drives all three, leaving them without a shared driver and almost certainly understating their correlation in any Monte Carlo. ~35% by end-2027, 55% by 2031, ~62% by 2036.

missing_risks.name: Lethal DPRK-ROK military exchange
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: An exchange of fire or attack between DPRK and ROK forces causing at least five combined military or civilian deaths, confirmed by either government or by the UN Command.
missing_risks.reasoning: The model prices a DPRK nuclear test but carries no Korean conventional risk at all, despite Korea having the richest recent base rate of lethal state-on-state incidents of any dyad it covers: Cheonan and Yeonpyeong (2010, ~50 deaths), the 2015 DMZ mine and artillery exchange, the 2020 liaison-office demolition, and repeated 2024-25 border-wall and GPS-jamming incidents. Roughly one qualifying event in 20 years plus the collapse of the 2018 inter-Korean military agreement gives ~5-6%/yr. It also matters structurally: the model names a pro-nuclear ROK president (2030 election) as 'the most likely proliferation trigger of the decade', and a lethal Northern provocation is the most plausible thing that elects one - so omitting it leaves the proliferation forecast without its main causal pathway. ~9% by end-2027, 30% by 2031, ~45% by 2036.

calibration.overall_bias:
The model is NOT uniformly over-forecasting drama. It over-forecasts the shocks it has recently read about and under-forecasts the slow institutional moves - the classic availability signature dressed up as base-rate discipline. The tell is structural: almost every risk carries a well-written base_rate_anchor whose implied rate is then multiplied by 3-10x on a one-line narrative justification, while the contrarian_case paragraphs repeatedly state the correct lower number ('a flat 3%/yr is defensible', 'I could easily be 15 points too high', 'I am 25 points too high') without the headline ever moving. He even names the bias in structural_uncertainties ('I may be systematically anchored on the last six months... my 2031 and 2036 cumulative numbers are collectively too high') and then does not act on it. Writing the self-critique is not the same as applying it; a reader should treat those contrarian paragraphs as the better-calibrated forecast roughly 30% of the time.

Recommended shrink is NON-UNIFORM. Applied to the odds ratio against the stated base rate, not to the probability:

(1) NARRATIVE-SHOCK CLUSTER - shrink 0.60. geopolitics_grid_cyberattack_nato (a 1M-person/24-hour outage has never occurred anywhere on earth, priced at 33% by 2036), geopolitics_dprk_nuclear_test (13%/yr implied against his own 8%/yr model and a nine-year drought), geopolitics_us_china_lethal_clash (priced off mechanisms its own wording excludes), geopolitics_unsc_permanent_expansion (4x the historical rate for an easier amendment, at minimum P5 comity).

(2) STRICT-CRITERION CLUSTER - shrink 0.80. Where the number reflects the vibe and the wording is harder than the vibe: geopolitics_ukraine_durable_ceasefire (180 clean days, whole front, no city strikes, while his own evidence points at a partial freeze with continued deep strikes), geopolitics_iran_regime_change (an IRGC-dominated Mojtaba consolidation resolves NO), geopolitics_iran_nuclear_weapon (assembled, confirmed, publicly assessed).

(3) SLOW-INSTITUTIONAL CLUSTER - EXPAND 1.35. The mirror image of (1): unglamorous, negotiable, reversible things get under-rated because they do not generate headlines. geopolitics_us_russia_strategic_arms_deal is the clearest case - the criterion admits a bare reciprocal political commitment announced by two heads of state, an instrument both leaders have already publicly floated, priced at 11% for 17 months. geopolitics_china_taiwan_quarantine_or_blockade is second - he argues quarantine dominates invasion and then prices it at only 2.3x invasion.

(4) ALREADY-HAPPENING CLUSTER - EXPAND 1.4. geopolitics_hormuz_major_closure is priced at 58% for an event his own continuous variable says is occurring now, corroborated by external July 2026 flow and transit data. When a discrete risk and its own continuous variable disagree about the present, the discrete risk is the one anchored to a stale narrative.

Net across the 18 discrete risks my revisions lower 11 figures and raise 8, so aggregate probability mass barely moves - a naive global shrink of about 0.95. That scalar is misleading and should not be applied. The real defect is dispersion and allocation, not level: the model spreads similar probability across wildly dissimilar evidence quality, over-weighting six months of news flow and under-weighting anything that requires a signature rather than a shooting. If a single figure is required for the shock cluster - which is what the question is really asking - use 0.70. Two further global points. First, the model has no correlation structure at all: the Iran campaign, Hormuz flow, Brent, Russian sanctions revenue, EU coalition cohesion and Iranian regime survival are one joint distribution reported as six independent marginals, which will badly understate tails in any simulation built on it. Second, the two genuinely first-order omissions - P5 nuclear-testing resumption and Putin succession - are both events the analyst demonstrably knows about, since one is implicit in his own New START narrative and the other is written verbatim into his structural_uncertainties. Knowing about a risk and pricing it are different acts, and this model consistently performs only the first. One credit where due: geopolitics_nuclear_use_in_anger (1 / 3.5 / 6, implying a near-constant ~0.65%/yr) is well-placed - above the superforecaster ~1%-by-2045 anchor and below the Metaculus community's implied ~1.2%/yr for detonation-in-war by 2050 - and I recommend no change to it. The Japan-China, Sahel, and US-NATO-withdrawal risks are likewise defensible as stated."

research.state_of_play:
As of late July 2026 the dominant near-term fact in this domain is a rapidly intensifying, possibly record-strength El Niño. I verified that NOAA CPC put El Niño emergence at 82% for May-Jul 2026 and 96% for Dec 2026-Feb 2027, that NOAA declared a "Super El Niño" underway on 11 June 2026 with a 63% chance of a "very strong" event, and that GFDL's July SPEAR run has all 30 ensemble members peaking at strengths competitive with the strongest events of the past century, peaking late 2026. ECMWF's median Niño3.4 peak is around +3.0C for December with high-end members near +4C. I treat the more extreme multi-model medians circulating (e.g. +3.59C) with skepticism: no event in 150 years of record has meaningfully exceeded +2.75C, and dynamical models have historically overshot super-event forecasts (2014 being the canonical bust). The physically defensible read is a very strong event that is more likely than not to rival 1997-98 and 2015-16, with a real chance of setting a record and a meaningful chance of underperforming the hype.

Global temperature has been in a relative lull. Verified: H1 2026 was the third-warmest start on record in all six major datasets, behind 2024 and 2025, at roughly 1.4C above pre-industrial. January was fifth-warmest (12.95C, +0.51C vs 1991-2020), April joint third (14.89C, +1.43C above pre-industrial), while May and June were both second-warmest globally as El Niño took hold. June was the hottest June on record for western Europe. Carbon Brief's record-year probability for 2026 rose from 19% in April to 35% in July; Polymarket prices 2026 at ~31% for warmest and ~60% for second-warmest, with ~85% odds on at least one record month. The critical implication is that 2027, not 2026, is the likely record year — the 2015/2016 analogue puts peak global response roughly a year after the Niño3.4 peak.

Ocean state is extreme. Global SST anomaly hit +0.5C on 30 June 2026, the highest ever for that date; H1 2026 was the second-warmest ocean half-year at ~20.94C. Ocean heat content set a record for the ninth consecutive year in 2025 (+23±8 ZJ, 0-2000m). In 2025, 89% of the global ocean saw at least one marine heatwave and 55% saw strong-or-worse. The fourth global coral bleaching event, declared April 2024, remains active; 84.4% of global reef area saw bleaching-level stress between Jan 2023 and Sep 2025. Every strong El Niño since 1998 has coincided with a global bleaching event, so reef outcomes in 2026-27 are likely to be historically bad.

Cryosphere: Arctic winter maximum on 15 March 2026 was 14.29 million km², statistically tied with 2025 for the lowest on record and 1.36 million km² below the 1981-2010 average. Antarctic sea ice, notably, rebounded — the 26 February 2026 minimum of 2.58 million km² ranked only 16th lowest, ending four years of record/near-record lows, driven by Weddell Sea wind anomalies rather than any thermodynamic reprieve. Greenland lost 139 Gt in the 2024-25 hydrological year. Sea level rise is running ~4.5-5.9 mm/yr with acceleration of ~0.83 mm/yr/decade.

Emissions have plateaued but not peaked. GCP put 2025 fossil CO2 at a record 38.1 GtCO2 (+1.1%); IEA put energy CO2 at 38.4 Gt (+0.4%) and forecasts power-sector emissions plateauing 2026-2030. China's emissions fell 0.3% in 2025 and have been flat-or-falling for 21 months. The remaining 1.5C budget is ~170 GtCO2, about four years. Mauna Loa CO2 was 431.44 ppm in June 2026; the 2026 annual mean is forecast at 429.4±0.6 ppm (+2.37 ppm). Methane reached ~1938 ppb at Mauna Loa in March 2026 and continues accelerating.

Policy has bifurcated. The US Paris withdrawal took effect January 2026 and EPA rescinded the 2009 endangerment finding on 12 February 2026 (effective 20 April), now in D.C. Circuit litigation. Countervailing: the ICJ's July 2025 advisory opinion was operationalized by UNGA resolution A/80/L.65 on 20 May 2026, and domestic courts in Costa Rica, France, the Netherlands, Brazil and Canada have already cited it. UNEP's 2025 Emissions Gap Report puts NDC-implied warming at 2.3-2.5C. COP31 convenes in Antalya 9-20 November 2026 under a Turkey/Australia split arrangement.

Not verified this session and drawn from pre-2026 knowledge: exact ERA5 2025 annual anomaly, IPCC AR7 timeline specifics, COP32 host, current RAPID AMOC transport values, and September 2026 Arctic minimum (not yet occurred).
