calibration.overall_bias:
Two opposite biases, plus one disqualifying factual error.

(1) FACTUAL: the model's oil/gas block is anchored to a stale 7 July 2026 EIA STEO snapshot and the analyst explicitly dismissed contradicting trackers as "stale or fabricated". Web verification says the opposite: the US struck Iran ~8 July (Al Jazeera, 8 Jul: "Oil surges as US strikes Iran, reversing return to pre-war prices"); Hormuz shipping "ground to a halt" as fighting resumed (Al Jazeera, 10 Jul); transits ran 10-15/day on 19-23 July against an ~88/day baseline (11-17%); Lloyd's List reports no >10,000 dwt vessel transiting the Southern Highway with AIS on since 7 July, ~75 tankers dark, war-risk premia at 8x pre-crisis and 6 P&I clubs withdrawing cover; Iran fired ballistic missiles at US bases on 28 July (CNBC, 28 Jul, WTI +4.4% to $82.73). Brent is ~$85-100, not the model's $72-74. The analyst applied the right epistemic instinct (distrust low-quality trackers) to the wrong target and let a report published two days before the escalation override the escalation itself. Every oil, gas and Gulf-security number needs a regime reset, not a shrink.

(2) OVER-forecasting on exotic peacetime shocks with zero-instance reference classes: grid cyber (0 OECD events in 16 yrs, rated 9% by 2027 = ~6.5%/yr), physical sabotage at 500k/24h (never achieved anywhere, largest ever ~45k, rated 7% by 2027 = ~5%/yr), firm load shed (~8-12%/yr base rate inflated to ~15%/yr). Suggested shrink factor for this class: 0.55-0.65.

(3) UNDER-forecasting on scheduled, recurring, boring policy machinery: Chinese REE controls at repeated annual decision points, REE export volume collapses (already nearly realised in 2025), and Western SMR delivery. Suggested inflation factor for this class: 1.25-1.35.

Also a systematic nominal-threshold inconsistency: inflation erosion is invoked to argue the $120 Brent number is too low, but the same logic is never applied to the $45 Brent floor or the $15,000 copper ceiling, where it cuts the other way.

adjustments.justification: The resolution criterion (transits <25% of the 2025 daily average for 14+ consecutive days at any point after 1 Aug 2026) is on the verge of resolving YES at the moment of writing. Verified: transits were 15/day on 19 July and 10/day on 23 July against an ~88/day baseline (11-17%); Lloyd's List reports no AIS-on transit of the Southern Highway by any vessel >10,000 dwt since 7 July; 6 P&I clubs have withdrawn cover and war-risk pricing is 8x pre-crisis. The condition has effectively been met continuously since ~7-10 July. Unless a durable settlement lands and traffic normalises within days, 14 consecutive sub-25% days in August is close to automatic. The 24% figure is not a calibration error, it is a state error: the analyst treated the 17 June truce as holding when the US struck Iran on 8 July and Iran fired ballistic missiles at US bases on 28 July.

Follows mechanically from the 2027 revision; only a small increment remains for later independent recurrences. Note the coherence trap the analyst avoided but for the wrong reason: once P(2027) is ~85%, the declining marginal hazard argument becomes nearly irrelevant to the cumulative.
Mechanical consequence of the above.

The stated evidence is wrong in a way that reverses its sign. The analyst claims the 2026 closure produced 'only a brief excursion above $120, not a sustained monthly average', treating this as powerful evidence of system slack. Statista puts the April 2026 Brent monthly average at $117.29 — it missed the threshold by $2.71, i.e. 2.3%. That is a near-miss, not a demonstration of slack, and it occurred with OECD stocks full and a ~2 Mb/d structural surplus. With the strait effectively re-closed since ~7 July, Brent already at $85-100, and a further 17 months of horizon, P(some month averaging >$120) is far above 14%. Conditional on a sustained re-closure (now ~85%), P($120 monthly average) is ~45-50% given the April precedent, which alone gives ~40pp.

Adds the analyst's own (correct) arguments they then failed to price: OPEC+ deliberately burning spare capacity to defend share through the late 2020s, non-OPEC plateau from Guyana/Brazil/US shale, and nominal-threshold erosion. Their contrarian case says 45-50% is defensible before accounting for the live closure; with it, ~58%.

$120 nominal in 2036 is ~$95 in today's money — roughly where Brent traded in mid-July 2026. Over a further decade containing at least one Gulf security cycle, an OPEC+ spare-capacity trough, and ~25% cumulative inflation, 42% is implausibly low. Note the original ordering was also near-degenerate against the collapse risk: 42% up and 48% down left only 10% for a decade inside the $45-120 band.

Conditioned on the wrong state. The 17% assumed Brent at $72-74 in a 2 Mb/d surplus with OPEC+ adding barrels; actual Brent is ~$85-100 with the strait re-closing and Gulf war-risk premia at 8x. Reaching a sub-$45 monthly average by end-2027 now requires both a full Gulf de-escalation AND an OPEC+ price war AND a demand disappointment, in 17 months. That is a conjunction of three, not one.

Modest trim. The surplus fundamentals are real and survive the shock, so the medium-horizon logic largely stands, but the near-term path is now blocked and the nominal threshold is eroding: $45 in 2031 is roughly $40 in today's terms, below almost every marginal-barrel cash cost outside OPEC core.

Inconsistent nominal treatment. The analyst explicitly argues that $120 in 2036 is only ~$95 real and therefore the upside number should be raised — but never applies the identical logic to the downside, where $45 in 2036 is ~$36 real. At ~2.5%/yr inflation, a sub-$45 nominal monthly print by 2036 requires a real oil price below anything seen outside March-April 2020. 48% is roughly 10 points too high.

The load-bearing evidence was flagged NOT VERIFIED by the analyst themselves ('TTF gas levels during the closure'), and the verified record undercuts the conclusion. TTF front-month jumped ~29% to just shy of EUR 70/MWh on 9 March 2026 (S&P Global) — the highest since January 2023 — i.e. it got 70% of the way to the threshold within days of Qatar halting. The resolution bar is a single trading day above EUR 100, not a sustained crisis, which is far easier than the 'crisis levels' framing implies (scope insensitivity in the low direction). With the strait re-closed as of late July, Qatari LNG at risk again, and the Q4 2026 heating season ahead with storage drawn, 14% is roughly half of what the wording supports. The analyst's own contrarian case says 25% is arguable; the live re-closure pushes it higher.

A single-day EUR 100 settle over a five-year window containing at least one cold winter, one Norwegian outage season, and continued Gulf/Russian escalation risk, given TTF already touched EUR 70 in 2026 and spent ~12 months above EUR 100 in 2021-22. Europe has swapped pipeline monopoly for global price-taking; in any Asian cold snap it must outbid JKM.

The declining-hazard profile from the LNG glut is right in direction but the glut is a 3-5 year phenomenon by the model's own feedback loop ('LNG glut creates its own demand', timescale 4 yrs, strength 0.6), which re-tightens the market by the early 2030s — exactly the period the model assigns the lowest hazard. Internally inconsistent.

Hazard-shape error. This is not a one-shot binary, it is a recurring decision point: each suspension is time-limited and must be affirmatively renewed. The analyst's own base rate says China extends 'roughly 60-65% of the time at decision points'. Compounding that over the ~5 annual decision points to end-2031 gives P(never snaps back) = 0.62^5 ~ 9%, i.e. P(YES) ~ 91%. Even allowing for a durable multi-year trade settlement and for leverage depreciation reducing Beijing's willingness to spend it, 62% is too low. The gap between 45% (2027) and 62% (2031) implies only ~31% cumulative snap-back hazard across four further decision points, versus ~85% under their own stated per-decision rate.

Same recurring-decision-point logic extended. The analyst also notes China 'has never permanently withdrawn a control regime once written' and that Beijing has an incentive to use the leverage before ex-China supply erodes it — both arguments push the long-horizon number up, not toward a 6-point increment over five years.

Scope insensitivity: the stated criterion is far weaker than the 'severe weaponisation / embargo' narrative attached to it. It asks only for >50% y/y decline in NdPr or heavy-RE exports to the US OR the EU for three consecutive months, per China customs. The April-June 2025 licensing squeeze — which the analyst characterises as merely 'throttling, stopping short of embargo' — produced US magnet/RE export declines widely reported near 75-90% y/y for two-plus months. Ordinary licensing-pipeline freezes clear this bar; a Taiwan-class rupture is not required. Given a ~45% chance the extraterritorial regime enters force by 2027 and that entry into force would itself freeze the licensing pipeline for weeks, 15% understates the wording badly. Also note the near-subset relation with energy_china_ree_extraterritorial_controls that the two numbers treat as near-independent.

Same scope correction, compounded over more decision points and rising Taiwan/semiconductor escalation risk. The 2025 precedent means the reference class is 'licensing friction severe enough to shut European auto lines', which has fired once in the last 18 months, not 'the 2010 Japan embargo', which fired once in 16 years.

Scope correction plus the horizon's accumulated rupture risk. The late-horizon decay from ex-China supply is real but the model's own china_ree_refining_share_pct variable only falls from 87% to a median 79% by 2031, so the leverage persists.

Base-rate violation driven by availability (Polish grid attack Dec 2025). Reference class: zero cyber-caused outages in any OECD country in 16 years despite thousands of documented intrusions; the largest confirmed cyber outage anywhere remains Ukraine 2015 at 225,000 customers for ~6 hours — less than half the customer threshold, in a wartime target with far weaker OT segmentation. 9% over 17 months implies ~6.5%/yr for an event that has never occurred, against the analyst's own stated unconditional rate of 'below 2%/yr'. The attribution requirement ('publicly confirmed by the relevant national CERT, regulator or system operator') tightens it further, as the analyst concedes.

25% by 2031 implies a sustained ~5%/yr hazard, ~2.5x the analyst's own adjusted unconditional rate, for a first-ever event with a demanding attribution gate. 16% (~3%/yr) already embeds a generous multiple on the pre-positioning evidence.
Proportional correction; the inverter-fleet attack-surface argument is genuinely good and justifies a rising hazard, so I keep the shape and cut the level.

Base-rate violation. The stated reference class is explicit: 5-8 notable OECD attacks in 13 years, none exceeding ~50,000 customers, zero at the 500k/24h threshold, base rate 'under 1%/yr'. The revision to 7% over 17 months is a ~5x multiple on a never-observed event, justified only by rising frequency of much smaller attacks — but the frequency of 45k-customer attacks says little about the 500k/24h tail, which requires multi-substation engineering coordination, and the largest observed event is an order of magnitude short on both axes simultaneously.

20% implies ~4%/yr sustained against a stated <1%/yr base rate. 13% retains a ~3x escalation multiple, which is generous given post-2013 spare-transformer reserve programmes explicitly target the duration leg of the criterion.
Proportional; the conflict-conditional tail is real and preserved in the rising shape.

22% over 17 months implies ~15%/yr against the analyst's own stated 8-12%/yr unconditional rate, and that base rate is itself flattered by counting three separate RTO events from the single Feb 2021 Uri episode. On an episode basis the record is 2 episodes in 26 years (2011, 2021) = ~8%/yr. Post-Uri winterisation in ERCOT and SPP, ~10 GW of ERCOT batteries covering the evening net-peak, and standard curtailable-load clauses in hyperscaler interconnection agreements (which shift the shed onto non-firm data-center load, outside the criterion) all cut the conditional probability.

54% by 2031 implies ~14%/yr sustained, i.e. no credit at all for the mitigations the analyst themselves lists in the contrarian case. 45% keeps the elevated-relative-to-history level (~11%/yr) that the queue backlog, turbine sell-out and transformer lead times genuinely justify.

Proportional; the hazard should ease after ~2031 as turbine and transformer bottlenecks clear, which the original profile does not really reflect (it adds 14pp over the final five years against 32pp over the prior four).

Directly inconsistent with the model's own continuous variable. global_solar_additions_gw has current_value 650, annual_drift 45, annual_vol 75 — implying a 2027 median of ~740 GW. Reaching 1,000 GW by 2027 is ~2.7 sigma on the model's own parameters, i.e. well under 5%, not 10%.

The clearest internal coherence violation in the model. The continuous variable gives 2031 p50 = 880 and p90 = 1,180 GW, so P(2031 additions >1,000) is roughly 25-30%; taking the union across 2028-2031 with a rising trend gets to perhaps 30-33%. The discrete risk asserts 58%. These cannot both be right. Either the discrete comes down to the mid-30s or the continuous drift (45 GW/yr, well below the 10-yr ~28% CAGR) must be raised substantially — and the analyst's own contrarian case argues the latter. I revise the discrete to 38% as the midpoint, but the model should be internally reconciled rather than split-the-differenced: pick one.
Continuous variable implies a 2036 median of ~1,100 GW, giving P(some year >1,000 by 2036) around 65-72%. 81% again runs ahead of the model's own distribution.

Two problems. (a) Resolution timing: 'IEA reports... at or before the stated year' — 2027 coal demand is not published until 2028, so only 2026 data can realistically resolve by end-2027, and 2026 is a year in which a four-month Gulf supply shock with LNG at crisis prices plausibly pushed Asian coal burn UP. (b) Base rate: only two multi-year declines since 1950, one of which fully reversed; a 3% fall from 2025 within one publishable year has essentially no precedent outside the post-Soviet collapse and 2020.

The analyst's own contrarian case argues 15 points too high and gives the reasons: non-power coal (~1/3 of demand, steel/cement/coal-to-chemicals) is near-inelastic, India plans a 46% coal capacity increase to 2030, ~80 GW commissioned in China in 2025 with 161 GW proposed, and every declared peak since 2014 has been premature. Also, the reporting-lag issue means the last resolvable year for a 2031 deadline is 2030, not 2031, which the 54% does not appear to net out. I cut 9 points rather than 15 because the continuous variable (p50_2031 = 8,470 vs 8,800 current, i.e. -3.75%) does support a coin-flip-or-better; the two should be revised together or the continuous drift made less negative.
Small trim for the same reporting-lag effect (last resolvable year is 2035) and for non-power coal's floor.

Inconsistent with the model's own continuous variable and with its own base rate. global_oil_demand_mbd has annual_drift +0.35 Mb/d and p50_2031 = 106.3 vs 104.5 today — a median path with no decline at all. Meanwhile the criterion is deliberately demanding: a y/y decline in a year with global real GDP growth above 2% and no Hormuz-class disruption. That has never happened in 61 years; all four historical declines were recession- or embargo-driven, and the exclusion filter strips exactly those. 42% within five years for an unprecedented event, on a median path that is still rising, is not supportable. Note also the 2026 exclusion now needs extending: 2026 is disqualified for the Feb-Jun shock, but the July re-closure likely disqualifies 2026 and possibly 2027 as well, further shrinking the resolvable window.

Direction is right and the EV mechanism is real, but the clean-resolution filter (>2% global GDP growth, no supply shock) will disqualify a meaningful fraction of candidate years — and the 2020s/2030s look shock-prone, not shock-free. 68% does not appear to price the filter.

Near-mechanically excluded: 2026 is already excluded by the model's own wording, the July re-closure makes 2027 a strong candidate for the same exclusion, and IEA full-year 2027 demand data are not published until 2028.

Under-forecast via an ill-fitting reference class. The base rate is drawn from gigawatt FOAK (Vogtle, Flamanville, OL3, HPC) whose overruns were driven by first-of-a-kind large-component fabrication, site-specific construction and new-entrant operators — precisely the factors Darlington BWRX-300 avoids (licensed BWR-derived design, factory-fabricated road-shippable modules, brownfield site, existing licensed operator, CNSC operating-licence application already filed March 2026). The portfolio also has multiple independent shots (Darlington, Natrium, X-energy/Dow Seadrift, RoPower Doicesti), so total failure by 2031 requires correlated slippage across all of them. The analyst's own contrarian case says 70% is respectable; 65% is the conservative version of that.

Near-arithmetically excluded. Three consecutive declines with the third at or before 2027 requires declines in 2025, 2026 and 2027. Global energy CO2 hit a record >38 Gt in 2025 with China ~1/3 of it and the model itself describes Chinese emissions as 'wobbling around a plateau since 2023' rather than declining — so the 2025 leg is not established. Additionally, 2027 Chinese data will not be published, let alone confirmed by IEA/CREA, until 2028-29, and the model's own structural-uncertainty section flags that NBS restates energy balances by several percent. 11% ignores both the arithmetic and the publication lag.

Revised down from 52. Base rate is literally zero occurrences since 1980, and the one near-miss (2014-16, two years) reversed on stimulus. Requiring three consecutive years with no hydro-drought rebound, no stimulus construction cycle and no coal-served AI buildout, resolved against data that get revised by several percent, is demanding. The 15FYP carbon-cap argument is genuinely strong in the other direction, which is why I only cut 8 points rather than more.

$40,000/t is ~+73% from ~$23,100/t. 19% over 17 months implies ~13%/yr against the analyst's own 9%/yr episode base rate, in a market whose supply is unusually elastic on a 12-18 month lag (Chinese lepidolite, African spodumene, DLE restarts) and where sodium-ion imposes a soft ceiling around $25,000/t for stationary storage. Momentum justifies some uplift over base rate, but not 1.5x. The 2031/2036 numbers (37/45) are defensible and I leave them.

Mild under-forecast at the long horizon. Global electrolysis went from roughly 0.1 GW to ~2.5 GW over 2015-2025, a ~25x decade; 2.5 to 25 GW by 2036 is a 10x decade, i.e. slower than the realised trend. The analyst's own contrarian points (5% displacement of the 90 Mt/yr grey hydrogen in ammonia/refining is already ~30 GW; Chinese alkaline capex ~1/4 of Western and systematically undercounted by Western trackers) support the higher figure. The 7%-realisation heuristic is correctly applied to the 2030 pipeline but is being over-extrapolated to a horizon six years beyond it.

The war-risk leg is live in a way the 4% does not reflect as of end-July 2026: US-Iran hostilities have resumed (US strikes 8 July, Iranian ballistic missile launches at US bases 28 July), and the analyst themselves notes Bushehr was reportedly within the conflict's target set, alongside continued Zaporizhzhia off-site-power losses. The post-1990 peacetime rate of ~2.8%/yr is the wrong anchor for a period with two active conflicts adjacent to operating reactors. The 2031/2036 figures (11/19) are internally coherent with a mildly declining hazard and I leave them.

coherence_violations: STATE ERROR PROPAGATING THROUGH THE WHOLE OIL BLOCK: the model asserts the Strait of Hormuz reopened and Brent is $72-74. Verified as of 28 July 2026: US strikes on Iran 8 July, Iranian ballistic missile launches at US bases 28 July, Hormuz transits 10-15/day vs ~88 baseline, no AIS-on transit of the Southern Highway by any vessel >10,000 dwt since 7 July per Lloyd's List, 6 P&I clubs withdrawing cover, Brent ~$85-100. The analyst dismissed the correct trackers as 'stale or fabricated' while anchoring on an EIA STEO published two days before the escalation. brent_crude_usd_bbl current_value=73 is wrong by 15-35%.

energy_solar_terawatt_year vs global_solar_additions_gw: the discrete risk says 58% chance of a 1,000 GW year by 2031, but the continuous variable (current 650, drift +45/yr, vol 75) puts the 2031 median at 880 with p90 at 1,180, implying only ~25-30% for 2031 and ~30-33% for the 2028-2031 union. A ~25-30 point contradiction between two objects in the same model.

energy_global_oil_demand_peak vs global_oil_demand_mbd: 42% probability of a y/y decline by 2031 sits against a continuous variable with positive drift (+0.35 Mb/d/yr) and a 2031 median (106.3) above today (104.5) — and the discrete additionally filters out all recession-driven declines, which are the only kind that has ever occurred.

NOMINAL-THRESHOLD ASYMMETRY: inflation erosion is invoked explicitly to argue the $120 Brent number is too low at the long horizon ('$120 in 2036 is roughly $95 in today's money') and again for copper, but is never applied to the $45 Brent floor, where the same arithmetic makes 48% by 2036 far too high ($45 in 2036 is ~$36 real). The same reasoning tool is used only when it raises the number.

energy_china_ree_extraterritorial_controls HAZARD SHAPE: 45% by 2027 rising to only 62% by 2031 implies ~31% cumulative snap-back hazard across four further annual decision points, versus ~85% implied by the analyst's own stated 60-65% per-decision extension rate. Recurring renewal deadlines were modelled as if the November 2026 date were the only one.

energy_ree_supply_cutoff (15% by 2027) treated as near-independent of energy_china_ree_extraterritorial_controls (45% by 2027), when entry into force of the extraterritorial regime would itself freeze the licensing pipeline and plausibly produce the >50% y/y three-month export decline the cutoff risk requires. The implied conditional P(cutoff | controls in force) is under 25%, which contradicts the 2025 precedent the analyst cites.

energy_oil_price_spike_120 reasoning is internally contradictory with the state_of_play: state_of_play says 'Brent ran from ~$75 to above $120 by April'; the risk reasoning says the April excursion was 'brief... not a sustained monthly average'. The actual April 2026 Brent monthly average was $117.29 — a 2.3% near-miss, which is evidence AGAINST the 'system slack' conclusion drawn from it.

RESOLUTION-TIMING GAP across at least four risks: energy_global_coal_demand_structural_decline, energy_china_emissions_sustained_decline, energy_global_oil_demand_peak and energy_hydrogen_scale_milestone all resolve on annual statistics published 6-18 months after the calendar year, so the last resolvable year for a 'by 2027' deadline is 2025 or 2026, not 2027. The model's own structural_uncertainties section identifies this problem and then none of the probabilities are adjusted for it.

energy_europe_gas_price_crisis rests on a premise the analyst themselves listed as NOT VERIFIED ('TTF gas levels during the closure'). The verified figure (TTF near EUR 70/MWh on 9 Mar 2026, highest since Jan 2023) is a near-miss that undercuts rather than supports the 14% figure.

energy_europe_gas_price_crisis assigns its LOWEST marginal hazard to 2031-2036, but the model's own 'LNG glut creates its own demand' feedback loop (timescale 4 years) says the glut re-tightens the market by the early 2030s. The hazard profile contradicts the stated mechanism.

Oil price branches: P(>$120 month by 2036) 42% + P(<$45 month by 2036) 48% = 90%, leaving only 10% for a decade in which Brent's monthly average never leaves the $45-120 band. Not strictly impossible, but combined with the asymmetric inflation treatment it means the two tails were sized independently and never checked against each other.

missing_risks.name: Loss of Russian uranium enrichment and conversion services to Western utilities
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: Rosatom/TENEX deliveries of enrichment (SWU) or conversion services to US and EU utilities fall by more than 70% year-on-year for four or more consecutive quarters, whether by sanction, counter-sanction or contract termination, per Euratom Supply Agency and US DOE/EIA reporting.
missing_risks.reasoning: The model's own structural_uncertainties section flags 'this model has no explicit Russia node, a significant omission', then does not add one. Rosatom supplies roughly 40% of global enrichment capacity and a similar share of conversion, and is the only commercial source of the HALEU that TerraPower Natrium and X-energy Seadrift require — both of which the model lists as 2030 scheduled events without pricing their fuel dependency. Western replacement capacity (Urenco expansions, Orano Georges Besse II, Centrus Piketon) is under construction but does not close the gap before the early 2030s. This risk sits directly upstream of energy_western_smr_first_power and of the uranium_spot_usd_lb variable and would move both, yet appears nowhere. Base rate: the 2022-2024 period already saw partial US import bans with waivers to 2028, so the trajectory is established and the question is timing, not direction.

missing_risks.name: Inverter-driven systemic grid collapse in a major OECD system
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: A frequency, voltage or oscillation event causes loss of supply to 5 million or more customers for 6 or more hours across a national or multi-national synchronous area in the OECD, with the official investigation identifying inverter-based resource dynamics, insufficient system inertia or protection mis-coordination as a primary or contributing cause.
missing_risks.reasoning: The model has a cyber blackout risk and a sabotage blackout risk but no ACCIDENTAL blackout risk — despite the fact that the only event in the reference class that has actually happened at scale is accidental. The April 2025 Iberian blackout cut power to roughly 60 million people across Spain and Portugal and is the single most consequential grid event of the decade, with IBR penetration and system-strength deficits central to the investigation. This is a strictly larger, strictly more frequent hazard than either of the two included ones (which have zero OECD instances between them at their thresholds), and it is rising mechanically with the 800 GW/yr of renewable additions the model celebrates. Omitting it while including two never-fired attack scenarios is a textbook availability bias: dramatic causes crowded out the base-rate-dominant one.

missing_risks.name: US data-center electricity demand growth collapses
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: US data-center electricity consumption grows less than 3% year-on-year in any calendar year, or declines, per EIA/LBNL reporting — versus the 15-20%/yr trend.
missing_risks.reasoning: The model states plainly that 'AI compute demand could be wrong by a factor of three in either direction, and it is the single largest new driver in this model', and that us_datacenter_electricity_twh is 'genuinely bimodal' and 'should be modelled with a regime switch' — then provides no discrete risk for the regime switch. This is the highest-leverage omission in the domain: a capex bust simultaneously deflates energy_us_firm_load_shed, uranium_spot_usd_lb, energy_copper_price_shock, gas turbine pricing, energy_western_smr_first_power economics and the entire 'grid scarcity' narrative. Without it, the model's shock risks are silently conditioned on the AI buildout persisting, and their correlation structure is invisible.

missing_risks.name: Major producing state imposes an export ban or nationalisation on a critical mineral
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: A country accounting for 20% or more of global mined supply of lithium, cobalt, nickel, copper or rare earths imposes an export ban, export quota cut of 30%+, or nationalisation/forced-equity measure that removes 15% or more of global supply for 3+ months.
missing_risks.reasoning: The model treats supply-side coercion as an exclusively Chinese phenomenon, but the highest-frequency events in the reference class are host-state actions: Indonesia's 2014 and 2020 nickel ore bans, Chile's 2023 lithium nationalisation framework, Mexico's 2022 lithium nationalisation, Zimbabwe's 2022 spodumene export ban, and the DRC's 2025 cobalt export ban followed by the 96,600 t quota — which the model records as a fact in state_of_play without generalising to a risk class. That is roughly 5-6 qualifying-scale events in 12 years across the group, i.e. a base rate well above most of the discrete risks that were included. Resource nationalism is also mechanically pro-cyclical with the price rises the model forecasts for copper and lithium.

missing_risks.name: EU ETS2 delayed, price-capped or materially diluted
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: The EU formally postpones ETS2's start beyond 2027, or amends the directive to impose a binding price ceiling below EUR 60/tCO2, or exempts a whole covered sector (buildings or road transport), before 31 December 2028.
missing_risks.reasoning: The model lists ETS2 as a scheduled event and explicitly calls delay or dilution 'a live possibility and a bellwether for European climate-policy durability' — then assigns no probability, so the bellwether cannot be scored. Base rate for EU carbon-policy retreat under cost-of-living pressure is high: the 2023-24 Green Deal rollbacks, the CAP/nature-restoration climbdowns, the CBAM simplification package, the 2025 automotive CO2 compliance-flexibility amendment, and the existing MSR price-containment mechanism. Given EU industrial power already runs at 2x US prices with network charges up 46% since 2019, and a pre-2029-election window, a majority probability is the right prior. Its absence leaves the model with no European policy-durability node at all.

missing_risks.name: Qatari LNG force majeure removing 15%+ of global LNG supply for 60+ days
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: QatarEnergy declares force majeure or otherwise suspends loadings such that Qatari LNG exports fall below 40% of their 2025 monthly average for 60 or more consecutive days, per Kpler/ICIS tracking, at any point after 1 Aug 2026.
missing_risks.reasoning: Already realised once inside the model's own state_of_play window — Qatar halted operations on 2 March 2026 and its energy minister said resumption would take 'weeks to months' — yet it exists in the model only as a consequence of Hormuz closure, never as a tracked risk with its own probability. It deserves separation because the gas and oil chokepoint consequences diverge sharply: oil has bypass infrastructure (Saudi East-West, ADNOC Fujairah) and SPR coordination, LNG has neither, so Qatari LNG is a strictly harder-bound chokepoint than Qatari or Emirati crude. This is the direct driver of energy_europe_gas_price_crisis and its omission is why that risk's probability is too low.

missing_risks.name: Grid equipment supply chain forces cancellation or multi-year deferral of major interconnection programmes
missing_risks.resolution_criteria: A G7 transmission system operator or major US RTO publicly defers or cancels 10 GW or more of already-approved interconnection or transmission capacity, citing large power transformer, HVDC converter or gas turbine unavailability as the stated primary cause.
missing_risks.reasoning: The model documents the inputs in detail — 5-year large-transformer lead times, GE Vernova sold out into 2029-30, turbine prices +195% vs 2019, 2,600 GW of queue — and builds a feedback loop around them, but converts none of it into a resolvable proposition. This is the model's biggest UNDER-forecast omission: it is a slow-moving near-certainty of exactly the type the analyst warns about elsewhere. Unlike the load-shed risk it does not require a weather trigger, only the continuation of already-observed lead times, and it is the mechanism by which the grid constraint actually binds on decarbonisation outcomes.

research.state_of_play:
The defining H1-2026 event, which I verified by search and which post-dates my training, is a large Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) epidemic in eastern DRC. DRC and Uganda declared the outbreak on 15 May 2026; WHO's Director-General determined it a PHEIC on 17 May 2026 (first IHR Emergency Committee 19 May). As of data through 26 July 2026, DRC reported 3,262 confirmed cases and 1,437 deaths (Ituri 2,901/1,207 across 28 of 36 health zones; North Kivu 314/204). Uganda had 20 cases/2 deaths and has been cleared; one case reached France, and a US aid worker was medevaced to Germany on 13 July. This is already the largest BDBV outbreak ever and, by growth rate, the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record — approaching the 3,470-case Kivu 2018-20 total in ~10 weeks rather than 23 months. The decisive difference: there is no licensed vaccine or therapeutic for Bundibugyo (Ervebo and mAbs are Zaire-specific), so the ring-vaccination tool that contained 2018-20 is unavailable. Oxford's ChAdOx1-BDBV enrolled its first volunteer 24 July 2026 and CEPI has committed >$60M across three candidates, but none will reach this outbreak. WHO's $115M appeal is ~40% funded. Reported declines in *suspected* cases appear to reflect surveillance/testing collapse rather than epidemiological retreat — a measurement caveat I flag strongly.

H5 avian influenza remains a slow-burn panzootic, not an acute crisis. Globally only 12 human A(H5N1) cases (3 deaths; Bangladesh, Cambodia, India) were reported 4 Aug 2025–10 Jun 2026; cumulative 1997-2026 is 1,022. US human cases total 71 since 2024 with 2 deaths — human infections have sharply decelerated from the 2024 dairy-worker surge. The world's first-ever human H5N5 case (Grays Harbor County, WA; confirmed 13 Nov 2025, died 21 Nov 2025) produced no secondary transmission. Animal-side, however, the reservoir keeps expanding: 1,166+ US dairy herds across 19 states as of 22 July 2026 (Idaho leads with 173), poultry detections in 12 states in June 2026, and D1.1/D1.2 genotype spillovers into cattle and swine alongside dominant B3.13. CDC's IRAT keeps recent 2.3.4.4b isolates at "moderate," public risk "low." Countermeasure capacity moved backwards: HHS terminated 22 BARDA mRNA projects (~$500M) in Aug 2025 including the $766M Moderna H5N1 award.

US public health institutions are in visible disarray. CDC's workforce is down roughly a third in about a year; the agency has had no Senate-confirmed director since Monarez's removal (Aug 2025), with acting director O'Neill and deputy Abraham both gone by late Feb 2026. ACIP was reconstituted and narrowed COVID, MMRV (split under age 4) and hepatitis B (birth dose moved to shared clinical decision-making) recommendations; a D. Mass. court stay on 16 March 2026 postponed the revised 2026 childhood schedule, largely reverting to January 2025 versions, and AAP now publishes a competing schedule. Congress rejected the proposed 53% CDC / 40% NIH cuts — the FY2026 Labor-HHS bill signed 3 Feb 2026 gave CDC $9.2B (flat) and NIH ~$48.7-49B (+$415M). Consequences are showing in measles: 2,295 confirmed US cases as of 22 July 2026, the most since 1991, with genomic evidence (lineage D8-9171) of unbroken domestic transmission since January 2025. PAHO's Regional Verification Commission reviews US elimination status in November 2026.

Global architecture is weaker. US withdrawal from WHO took effect January 2026; WHO cut its 2026-27 programme budget from $5.3B to $4.2B and still faces roughly a $1.7B gap. Amended IHR entered into force 19 Sept 2025 with 11 rejections including the US. The Pandemic Agreement (adopted May 2025) is stalled pending its PABS annex — IGWG7 concluded July 2026 without agreement, IGWG8 runs 14-18 Sept 2026, and the outcome is slated for WHA80 (May 2027) or an earlier special session. Financing: Gavi 6.0 raised >$9B against $11.9B; Global Fund GC8 ~$11B against $18B; international HIV financing fell 18% to $7.3B in 2025. UNAIDS (27 July 2026) reported 1.2M new HIV infections and 570,000 AIDS deaths in 2025 — record lows, but described as "extremely fragile." Malaria deaths rose to 610,000 (2024); TB killed 1.23M (2024). WUENIC (15 July 2026) put 2025 DTP3 at 85% and zero-dose children at 13.5M. Respiratory season 2025-26 was an H3N2 subclade-K drift year (~11M US illnesses, 120k hospitalizations, 5,000 deaths by early Jan 2026; European VE 25-45%); COVID is quiescent with NB.1.8.1 dominant and ~1,200 US weekly admissions in mid-July 2026. GLP-1 use hit 12.4% of US adults (June 2026) and Gallup-measured obesity fell to 36.4% from a 39.9% peak. I could NOT verify current Metaculus/Polymarket H5 pandemic odds, current 2026 Lassa/Oropouche figures, or post-March 2026 CDC leadership resolution.

scheduled_events.why_it_matters: The single largest branch point for US vaccine policy, WHO membership, PEPFAR, and biomedical research funding in this horizon.
